title: BOM Cost and Component Analysis
problem: Hardware engineers manually calculate Bill of Materials costs across hundreds of components, factoring in quantity discounts, lead times, and alternate parts. Spreadsheet errors lead to budget overruns discovered late in development. A single miscalculated BOM line can cascade into thousands of dollars of NRE waste.
who: Hardware engineers managing BOM for PCB and system designs

skill_spec.name: BOM Cost Calculator
skill_spec.one_liner: Calculates total BOM cost with quantity tiers, NRE allocation, and per-unit manufacturing cost breakdown

inputs.name: components
inputs.label: List of components (part number, unit cost, quantity)

outputs.name: cost_breakdown
outputs.label: Cost breakdown by category (ICs, passives, connectors, PCB, assembly)

outputs.name: margin_analysis
outputs.label: Margin analysis at target retail price

skill_spec.formula_hint: per_unit = (sum(component_cost * qty) + pcb_fab + assembly) + (nre / production_volume). Category breakdown by component type. Margin = (retail - per_unit) / retail * 100

example_queries: Calculate BOM cost for a board with 150 components at 10,000 unit volume with $50,000 NRE
What's my per-unit cost if I have $12.50 in ICs, $3.20 in passives, $8 PCB, and $5 assembly at 5,000 units?
Break down manufacturing cost for a 500-unit prototype run vs 50,000 production run

title: Power Budget and Thermal Dissipation Calculation
problem: Engineers must calculate power consumption across all components on a board to size power supplies, regulators, and thermal solutions. Errors in power budgeting lead to thermal throttling, system instability, or costly board respins. Each iteration costs weeks and tens of thousands in prototype fabrication.
who: PCB and system-level hardware engineers designing power delivery networks

skill_spec.name: Power Budget & Thermal Calculator
skill_spec.one_liner: Calculates total power consumption, per-rail power budgets, thermal dissipation requirements, and heatsink sizing

inputs.name: components
inputs.label: Components with voltage rail and current draw (typ/max)

outputs.name: total_power_w
outputs.label: Total system power (Watts, typical and max)

outputs.name: regulator_sizing
outputs.label: Recommended regulator current rating per rail

skill_spec.formula_hint: P_rail = sum(V * I_component). P_total = sum(P_rail / efficiency). Theta_sa = (T_jmax - T_ambient) / P_dissipated - Theta_jc. Regulator headroom = I_max * 1.2

example_queries: Calculate power budget for a board with 3.3V rail at 2A, 1.8V at 5A, and 12V at 1.5A
What heatsink do I need for a 15W SoC with Tj max 105C in 40C ambient?
Size my voltage regulators for a design with 6 power rails

title: PCB Trace Width and Impedance Calculation
problem: Engineers need to calculate trace widths for current carrying capacity and controlled impedance for high-speed signals. Manual calculations using IPC-2152 charts are time-consuming and error-prone. Incorrect impedance causes signal integrity failures requiring expensive board respins.
who: PCB layout engineers and hardware designers working on high-speed designs

skill_spec.name: PCB Trace Width & Impedance Calculator
skill_spec.one_liner: Calculates PCB trace width for current capacity per IPC-2152 and controlled impedance for microstrip/stripline geometries
skill_spec.formula_hint: IPC-2152: I = k * dT^0.44 * A^0.725 (A = cross section area). Microstrip Z0 = (87/sqrt(Er+1.41)) * ln(5.98*h/(0.8*w+t)). Stripline Z0 = (60/sqrt(Er)) * ln(4*h/(0.67*pi*(0.8*w+t)))

example_queries: What trace width do I need for 3A on a 1oz copper inner layer with 10C rise?
Calculate microstrip width for 50 ohm impedance on FR-4 with 0.2mm dielectric height
What's the differential impedance for two 5-mil traces with 5-mil spacing on 4-layer stackup?

title: FCC Part 15 EMC Pre-Compliance Checklist
problem: Hardware products must pass FCC Part 15 emissions testing before sale in the US. Engineers often discover compliance failures during expensive third-party testing ($5,000-$15,000 per test), requiring redesign and retesting. A structured pre-compliance checklist prevents costly late-stage failures.
who: Hardware engineers preparing products for FCC certification

skill_spec.name: FCC Part 15 Pre-Compliance Checklist
skill_spec.one_liner: Step-by-step EMC design review and pre-compliance checklist to maximize chances of passing FCC testing on first attempt
steps: Step 1: Classify device - intentional radiator (Part 15 Subpart C) vs unintentional radiator (Subpart B) vs digital device (Class A industrial or Class B consumer)
Step 2: Review PCB layout - verify ground plane continuity, no splits under high-speed traces, proper decoupling cap placement
Step 3: Check clock signal routing - shortest paths, series termination resistors, avoid routing near board edges
Step 4: Verify I/O connector filtering - common mode chokes, TVS diodes, proper shield grounding on all external connectors
Step 5: Review power supply design - input filtering, snubber circuits, spread-spectrum clocking enabled
Step 6: Check enclosure shielding - gasket continuity, vent hole sizing (< lambda/20), cable shield grounding
Step 7: Perform pre-scan with near-field probe - identify hot spots above FCC limits
Step 8: Document test configuration - cable routing, peripheral connections, operating modes per FCC test procedure
Step 9: Prepare FCC filing documents - schematics, block diagram, operational description, label placement
Step 10: Submit to accredited test lab with all required documentation and samples
warnings: Warning: Class B (consumer) limits are 10 dB stricter than Class A - verify correct classification
Warning: FCC fines up to $100,000 per violation for marketing non-compliant devices
Warning: All cable assemblies used during testing must match production configuration

example_queries: What do I need to check before sending my PCB design for FCC testing?
Walk me through FCC Part 15 pre-compliance for a consumer IoT device
What are the most common reasons hardware fails FCC EMC testing?

title: Decoupling Capacitor Selection and Placement
problem: Selecting the right decoupling capacitors and placement strategy for power integrity is critical but time-consuming. Engineers must consider IC requirements, frequency ranges, ESR/ESL characteristics, and placement constraints. Poor decoupling causes power integrity failures, noise coupling, and costly debugging.
who: PCB designers and hardware engineers working on digital designs

skill_spec.name: Decoupling Capacitor Calculator
skill_spec.one_liner: Calculates optimal decoupling capacitor values, quantities, and target impedance for power delivery network design

inputs.name: num_power_pins
inputs.label: Number of power pins on IC

outputs.name: decoupling_caps
outputs.label: Recommended decoupling cap values and quantities

skill_spec.formula_hint: Z_target = V_ripple / I_transient. C_bulk = I * dt / dV. BW = 0.35 / rise_time. Cap per pin with ESL consideration. Placement: < lambda/20 at max frequency

example_queries: Calculate decoupling for an FPGA with 5A transient current on 1.0V core rail with 3% ripple
What's my target impedance for a 1.8V rail with 2A switching current?
How many 100nF caps do I need for a processor with 64 power pins?

title: RoHS and REACH Compliance Verification
problem: Hardware engineers must verify that all components in their BOM comply with RoHS restricted substance limits and REACH SVHC requirements. Non-compliance can block product sales in the EU and result in costly component substitutions late in development. Tracking compliance across hundreds of components is tedious.
who: Hardware engineers and compliance teams managing product certifications

skill_spec.name: RoHS/REACH Compliance Verification Checklist
skill_spec.one_liner: Step-by-step verification process for ensuring BOM compliance with RoHS and REACH substance restrictions
steps: Step 1: Identify applicable regulations - RoHS 2 (EU 2011/65/EU), RoHS amendments, REACH (EC 1907/2006), and any customer-specific requirements
Step 2: Export full BOM with manufacturer part numbers and supplier information
Step 3: For each component - obtain RoHS compliance declaration from manufacturer datasheet or compliance database
Step 4: Check for RoHS exemptions - verify applicable exemptions (Annex III/IV) and expiration dates
Step 5: Verify REACH SVHC (Substances of Very High Concern) - check latest SVHC candidate list against component materials
Step 6: Check solder and surface finish - verify lead-free solder compatibility, check for tin whisker risk
Step 7: Review PCB laminate and substrate materials - verify halogen-free requirements if applicable
Step 8: Document compliance evidence - collect certificates, declarations, and test reports per component
Step 9: Create compliance matrix spreadsheet with part number, status, exemption, and evidence reference
Step 10: Prepare Declaration of Conformity for the finished product
warnings: Warning: RoHS exemptions have expiration dates - verify current validity
Warning: REACH SVHC candidate list is updated twice per year - recheck before each product release
Warning: Solder paste and flux are often overlooked - these must also be RoHS compliant

example_queries: Walk me through RoHS compliance verification for a new PCB design with 200 components
What are the current RoHS restricted substances and their limits?

title: Prototype Bring-Up Procedure
problem: First power-on of a new prototype board is high-risk - incorrect bring-up sequence can damage expensive components or mask design bugs. Engineers rely on tribal knowledge and experience rather than systematic procedures. A missed step during bring-up can destroy a $5,000+ prototype board.
who: Hardware engineers performing first-article prototype bring-up and validation

skill_spec.name: Prototype Board Bring-Up Procedure
skill_spec.one_liner: Systematic bring-up checklist for safely powering on and validating a new prototype PCB from visual inspection through functional testing
steps: Step 1: Visual inspection - check solder joints under microscope, look for bridges, missing components, polarity errors, BGA alignment
Step 2: Continuity checks - verify power and ground nets are not shorted (measure resistance between all power rails and GND)
Step 3: Verify power supply connections - confirm correct voltage at regulator inputs with board unpowered
Step 4: Current-limited power-on - apply power through current-limited supply, start at reduced voltage, monitor current draw
Step 5: Power rail verification - measure all voltage rails with multimeter, verify within spec (typically +/-5%)
Step 6: Power sequencing - verify power-up sequence matches IC requirements using oscilloscope
Step 7: Clock verification - probe all clock outputs, verify frequency and amplitude
Step 8: Reset and boot - verify reset circuit timing, check processor boot indicators (LEDs, UART output)
Step 9: JTAG/debug interface - establish debug connection, verify processor ID, read device registers
Step 10: Peripheral bring-up - systematically test each interface (I2C scan, SPI loopback, UART echo, Ethernet link)
Step 11: Thermal check - run stress test, monitor temperatures with thermal camera or thermocouples
Step 12: Document all measurements and anomalies in bring-up log
warnings: Warning: ALWAYS current-limit power supply during first power-on - set limit to 50% of expected draw
Warning: Check for shorted power rails BEFORE applying power - a shorted rail can destroy multiple ICs instantly
Warning: If current draw exceeds expected value, IMMEDIATELY remove power and investigate

example_queries: Give me a bring-up checklist for a new FPGA development board prototype
What's the safe procedure for first power-on of a prototype with DDR4 memory?
What should I check before and during board bring-up to avoid damaging components?
